act: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 6 (Editor's Draft, 28 April 2026)

en.title: CSS Cascade 6: an example of overlapping scopes in §3.5.1 does not follow the current definition of scoping limits
en.summary: The last block of example #example-463550a5 uses to ([data-scope] > *) and says both sections are part of the outer scope. Under §3.5.2 and §3.5.4 the scope end is an ordinary selector list, so both children of the outer section, a p and the inner section, are scoping limits and are out of scope. The example holds only if the scope end is matched relative to :scope, which open issue 13290 proposes; the note was sent there as a comment.
en.impact: With the example's HTML, the current text applies section { background: snow } to no section and p { color: red } to no p; the example says the inner section is styled by both scopes.
en.correction: Once issue 13290 is resolved, check the example against the chosen definition, for example by using to (:scope [data-scope] > *).

quotes.text: However, authors can use the child combinator and universal selector to create scope boundaries that overlap, such that the inner scope root is part of both scopes:

quotes.source: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 6, Editor's Draft of 28 April 2026 (W3C CSS Working Group)
quotes.text: both sections are part of the outer scope

quotes.source: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 6, Editor's Draft of 28 April 2026 (W3C CSS Working Group)
quotes.text: For each scope created by a scoping root, its scoping limits are set to all elements that are descendants of the scoping root and that match <scope-end>, interpreting :scope and & exactly as in scoped style rules.

quotes.source: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 6, Editor's Draft of 28 April 2026 (W3C CSS Working Group)
quotes.text: It is not an inclusive descendant of a scoping limit.
